title: Effacement
hook: "others will be cruel; we will not be cruel here": forty-four resolves (MN 8)

segments.voice: Yesterday: upakkilesa, the stains, and the cloth that takes dye once it's clean. Your line: clean cloth takes dye.

In almost any group there comes a moment when someone says: everyone does it. Everyone pads the expense report a little. Everyone talks about the boss when she's out of the room. Everyone's a bit cruel online. It's hard to argue with, mostly because it's often a little true. A discourse in the Middle-Length Sayings has an answer to it, set out forty-four times.
screen: `EVERYONE DOES IT.` → `HARD TO ARGUE WITH.` → `AN ANSWER, FORTY-FOUR TIMES.`

segments.voice: MN 8, the Sallekha. A monk named Mahacunda asks how to let go of the many views people hold about the self and the world. The Buddha's answer starts somewhere unexpected. A monk might reach the jhanas, the deep meditative states, and think he's effacing. He isn't, the Buddha says; those are pleasant abidings, peaceful abidings, here and now. Sallekha comes from a verb meaning to scrape away, to pare down: the slow whittling of what doesn't belong. Then the refrain. Others will be cruel; we will not be cruel here: that is how you should efface. Others will kill living beings; we won't. Others will take what isn't given; we won't. Others will speak falsely, maliciously, harshly, idly; we won't. Others will be envious, stingy, deceitful, arrogant, hard to correct; we won't. Others will cling to their own views and let go only with difficulty; we won't. Forty-four in all. Two things stand out. The refrain never adds: and they're terrible. It draws a line around your own conduct. And it doesn't wait for everyone else to agree first. The Buddha gives a picture: as there might be an uneven road, and an even road to go around it, so not being cruel is the even road around cruelty. The sutta ends with a line he repeats to many students: here are the roots of trees, here are empty huts. Meditate. Don't delay, or you'll regret it later.
screen: `JHANAS ARE NOT EFFACEMENT.` · `SALLEKHA — PARING DOWN.` · `OTHERS WILL; WE WON'T, HERE.` · `THE EVEN ROAD AROUND.` · then, large: `OTHERS MAY, WE WON'T.`

segments.voice: Let the refrain run quietly, one line per breath: others may be harsh, I won't be harsh here; others may gossip, I won't gossip here; others may cling to their views, I won't cling here. Then drop the words, and keep the one resolve that fits your week, like a smooth stone in your pocket.
Sallekha. Effacement: paring away what's unhelpful, line by line, whatever others are doing.
Your line: others may, we won't. No waiting for everyone else to agree. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Theravada teachers often use the Sallekha Sutta's refrain as a model for personal resolves, and monastic training emphasizes keeping one's own conduct whatever others around one do.

fork.setup: everyone at work pads their expense reports a little. in the spirit of MN 8, what's the line?
options: everyone does it, so it's fine
fork.reveal: the refrain doesn't judge the others or wait for them. it simply says: here, we won't. that's effacement.

original.note: Pali sallekha: effacement, paring down; from a verb meaning to scrape or pare.

trapdoor: what you thought: effacement, like being shy or self-effacing.
what it means: paring away unhelpful habits, whatever the people around you do.
what a scholar hears: the sutta's closing words, roots of trees and empty huts, meditate and don't delay, recur as the Buddha's parting instruction in several discourses.

chat.meaning: MN 8's refrain, others will, we won't here, never condemns the others and doesn't wait for anyone else to agree first.
